title: Stamp Book
concept: After this one you can watch a grudge being collected one coupon at a time, and you can decline the cash-in.
bookIdea: Trading stamps are racket feelings, such as held resentments, saved up instead of said at the time, and a game's payoff is the moment they are traded in for a free blow-up.
bookSource: Scripts People Live, ch. 1; TA Today, ch. 1 and 21

opener.setting: Monday to Sunday, 9:00pm. Your room in apartment 3B, Hawthorn Court, by the bus stop. Mum is 600 km away, on the phone.

lines.text: “Four days and not one call. Saying nothing, I know. Just counting.”
lines.cue: pen tapping a notebook by the phone

lines.text: “Your mother's counting again. Let her count.”
lines.cue: in the background, the telly on mute

opener.ask: When someone keeps a tally of what you owe them, what do you do with the tally?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Some lines are plain complaints, said once. Others are grudge coupons, kept back in a private book for later. Pick the one that is being kept back.

items.text: “The bathroom tap's dripping. Can someone look at it this weekend, please?”
items.cue: looking at the tap, not at anyone
options: A grudge coupon: kept back, to be cashed in later
A plain complaint: said once, then let go
items.why: It names one thing, the tap, and asks for one thing, a look this weekend. Once someone agrees, the complaint is finished, and nothing is kept back for later.

traps.0: Reading it as a coupon would treat a simple request as a bill. Sam would feel counted, the tap would keep dripping, and the next request would arrive carrying this one along with it.

items.example:
A housing society notice board, Friday.
Resident: “The lift is out again. Can the office send someone before Monday, please?”
Office: “We'll send a man on Saturday.”

items.text: “Noted. That's the second deck this month that landed late. I'll keep it in mind.”
items.cue: not looking up from his screen, pen capped
options: A grudge coupon: kept back, to be cashed in later
A plain complaint: said once, then let go
items.why: 'I'll keep it in mind' is a coupon. It says nothing about the deck in front of him, and it files the late deck for a later day. The line is kept back, and the cash-in is still to come.

traps.1: Taking it as a plain complaint would answer the deck and drop the count. You would promise to send the next one early, Daniel would say fine, and the second late deck would simply become the third in his book.

items.example:
A school bake sale, Saturday.
Mum: “Noted. That's the second time your cake's been late. I'll remember.”
Son: “Right. Fine.” Nothing else is said, and the cakes are still late in May.

items.text: “It's fine. I'll do the dishes. I always do the dishes.”
items.cue: already at the sink, the tap running, the cloth put down hard
options: A plain complaint: said once, then let go
A grudge coupon: kept back, to be cashed in later
items.why: 'I always do the dishes' is said as a fact, but it is a count. Every pile she washes and every silence she keeps adds one more line to the book, so the coupon goes in and stays there.

traps.0: Taking it as a plain complaint would answer the dishes and leave the count alone. Sam would dry a plate and say sorry, and the next pile would bring the same line back with all the old ones behind it.

items.example:
A shared office kitchen, Wednesday.
Colleague: “I'll clean the kettle. I always clean it, nobody else does.”
She rinses the kettle hard and does not look round.

items.text: “My son didn't ring on my birthday. I won't say a word about it. I'm just noticing, that's all.”
items.cue: not looking up from the newspaper
options: A grudge coupon: kept back, to be cashed in later
A plain complaint: said once, then let go
items.why: 'I won't say a word about it' and 'I'm just noticing' are the tells. Nothing is asked for today, and the son is not asked anything at all. The line goes into the book, for a day when it can be cashed in on him, or on her.

traps.1: Taking it as a complaint about the birthday would make the call the topic. You would ask whether he is coming for the holiday weekend, and the coupon would stay in the book, because nothing you said could ever pay it off.

items.example:
A WhatsApp family group, Sunday.
Cousin: “Nobody mentioned my exam result. Not that I'm bothered. I'm just saying.”
Nobody replies to that one, and the exam comes up again over the holiday weekend.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Two scenes. Each line is a chance to keep a coupon or to put it down, and a coupon you never spend is one the other person cannot cash in.

items.title: Monday to Sunday, 9:00pm, the phone
items.setting: Mum is 600 km away, on speaker by the kitchen sink. The call comes in at nine every evening, and she writes in a notebook while she talks.

beats.text: “You didn't call on Sunday. Your cousin rang me on hers, you know. I said you were busy. Busy.”
beats.cue: Coupon one. Pen tapping the notebook.

lines.text: “I missed Sunday, Mum, and that's on me. Are you cross, or are you worried?”
lines.outcome: She stops writing. “Worried. Both. Mostly worried,” she says.
lines.why: You own the miss in one line and ask which feeling is under it. A plain question gives the feeling somewhere to go, so no coupon is added to the book.

lines.text: “I was busy, Mum. Work's been mad this month.”
lines.outcome: “Busy,” she repeats, and writes the word down.
lines.why: This is true, but it answers the count and not the feeling. The word goes in the notebook and waits for the next call.

lines.text: “You've got a cousin who rings every Sunday. Maybe ask her why she has time.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Mum closes the notebook and says the rice is burning.
lines.why: This pays a coupon back in kind, and it turns the count into a fight about who is the better child.

beats.text: “Dad said we're fine on the phone, but his voice was grey. You'd know if you rang him, you know.”
beats.cue: Coupon two. Turning back a page to find the last one.

lines.text: “You're right. I'll ring Dad on Friday, and I'll ring you on Saturday. Did he say what's wrong?”
lines.outcome: She pauses. “Only that he's tired. He won't say more.”
lines.why: You take the part that is yours, name the days, and ask for what he said. A dated plan closes one coupon instead of opening a second.

lines.text: “Dad's always fine, Mum. You know how he is.”
lines.outcome: “That's just it,” Mum says. “Nobody asks him.”
lines.why: This brushes the feeling off, so Mum hears that nobody is going to ask. The coupon goes in the book under a new heading.

lines.text: “I'm not the one who made him grey. Ask him yourself.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Mum says, “Right. So it's me, then,” and the line goes quiet.
lines.why: This hands the blame to someone who is not on the call. It gives Mum a reason to keep the notebook open for good.

beats.text: “Your aunt asked if you're getting married. I said you're too busy for that, too. She laughed. It wasn't funny.”
beats.cue: Coupon three. Writing fast, the pen pressing hard.

lines.text: “I'd rather you didn't speak for me, Mum. Tell me what it was like to be asked about me.”
lines.outcome: Mum goes quiet. “Embarrassed,” she says at last. “I wanted to have something good to say.”
lines.why: You refuse to be spoken for, and you ask for the feeling under the joke. That keeps you the one who speaks, and it gives her a real thing to say in place of a coupon.

lines.text: “It's fine, Mum. Auntie means well.”
lines.outcome: “She does,” Mum agrees, and writes something down.
lines.why: It is kind, but it closes the topic on her side. The coupon stays in the book for later.

lines.text: “Stop keeping score for everybody. It's exhausting.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Mum's pen stops too, and she says nothing for a long time before goodnight.
lines.why: Naming her as the problem is a sting. It gives her a chance to say she was only worried, and the trap keeps running.

beats.text: “Is something wrong at the job? You sound flat. Or is it me? I'm just the one who keeps asking.”
beats.cue: Coupon four. Pen down, then up again.

lines.text: “It's a bit of both, I think. I'm tired, and I'm sorry I've been short with you. Can we talk properly on Sunday?”
lines.outcome: “Sunday, properly,” she says. “Yes. I'd like that.”
lines.why: You name your part and your tiredness, then set a time for the real talk. A named time is what closes a coupon.

lines.text: “It's not you, Mum. Work's just work.”
lines.outcome: “If you say so,” she says, not sure she believes it.
lines.why: Kind, but flat. It denies the question and does not answer it, so she keeps the coupon and waits.

lines.text: “You always make it about you, Mum. Every single call.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. She says she is going to bed, and the line goes dead before you can answer.
lines.why: This cashes a coupon in on her, and it lets her be the one who was hurt. From here on, both of you are playing.

beats.text: “So. Four coupons this week. I'm not angry. When you're ready, you'll know what you owe me.”
beats.cue: Cash-in. The notebook open at a clean page.

lines.text: “Mum, you're doing the notebook again. Tell me what you want from me, plainly, and I'll try to give it.”
lines.outcome: The notebook goes face down. “I want you to ring on Sunday,” she says. “Every Sunday. That's all.”
lines.why: You stop the count and ask for the want, not the debt. A plain want can be met, and a coupon can only be paid off.

lines.text: “Fine. I'll ring every Sunday. I promise.”
lines.outcome: “Good,” she says, and writes Sunday in the book with a line under it.
lines.why: A promise pays the coupons this time, and the book stays open for next week. Nothing was asked for, so nothing was really given.

lines.text: “I owe you four calls and a trip home, and I'll never be enough for you.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Mum says, “Don't say that, love,” and the line goes quiet.
lines.why: This cashes the whole book in on yourself. Mum gets to comfort you, and the count goes on without anyone looking at it.

items.payoff: Sunday, 9:40pm. Mum cashes the whole book in at once: every coupon since Monday, read out in order. The call ends before anyone can answer the last one.

fallout.them: Mum does not ring on Monday, and the notebook is still open on the kitchen table.

items.title: Thursday to Friday, 7:30am, the kitchen
items.setting: Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B. The rent is due on Friday, the milk has gone off again, and Maya keeps her count on the back of a takeaway menu.

beats.text: “It's fine. The milk's off, I'll pour it away. I'll do it. I always do it.”
beats.cue: Coupon one. Pouring the milk down the sink without looking up.

lines.text: “Leave the milk, Maya. Sit down for five minutes. What's been the worst bit of your week?”
lines.outcome: She stops with the carton in her hand. “The shifts,” she says, and sits, surprised she's allowed to.
lines.why: You stop the chore and ask about her week, not her thanks. That gives her a seat, and the count loses a coupon.

lines.text: “Thanks. Do you want tea?”
lines.outcome: She nods, puts the kettle on, and keeps the count to herself.
lines.why: Kind, and it helps, but it thanks her for the chore and leaves the count where it was.

lines.text: “You always do it, Maya. Sam doesn't even notice.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. She says it's easier to do it herself, and she shuts the fridge door hard.
lines.why: This spends a coupon on Sam, and it hands her the job of defending him. The count now has a target.

beats.text: “Sorry, sorry. Milk tomorrow, rent on Friday, promise. You're the best, you know.”
beats.cue: Coupon two. Maya writes on the menu without looking at him.

lines.text: “You've said Friday before. What's the one thing you can do tonight?”
lines.outcome: Sam looks at his phone and says he'll send half now. “Half now,” he says, to himself.
lines.why: You ask for one real action tonight, not a promise for Friday. A promise is a coupon, and a transfer closes it.

lines.text: “It's fine, Sam. Just do it on Friday.”
lines.outcome: “Friday, yes,” he says, already halfway to his room.
lines.why: It sounds generous, but it takes the count on yourself and accepts a promise you have heard before.

lines.text: “Friday, Friday, every month. You never change.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam says nothing at all, and his door shuts.
lines.why: This sting gives him the chair he always sits in, and the trap has a fresh round before the flat wakes up.

beats.text: “The rent's due today. It's been due all week. I've been doing the sums on the back of this menu.”
beats.cue: Coupon three. Holding up the menu, the columns in pen.

lines.text: “I'd rather pay you on time than hear the sums again. What's the number? I'll send it by six.”
lines.outcome: She reads out the number. It is more than you thought, and she says six is fine.
lines.why: You turn the sums into a number and a time, and you take the piece that is yours. A named time closes the coupon.

lines.text: “Okay. Sorry about the sums.”
lines.outcome: She nods, folds the menu, and the sums go back in her pocket.
lines.why: A sorry closes the moment and keeps the amount hidden. The count goes on, out of sight, for next month.

lines.text: “A list on a menu? Good to know where I stand, then.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Maya puts the menu in the bin, then takes it out again.
lines.why: This sneers at the count, so she has to defend it. It is a sting, and it gives her one more reason to keep the menu.

beats.text: “It's fine. I'll cover it this month and move my things out of the shared fridge. I'm used to it.”
beats.cue: Cash-in. Zipping her bag, the menu folded inside.

lines.text: “Don't cover it, Maya. Tell him what you need, then let him answer.”
lines.outcome: She stops with the bag half zipped and says the milk is someone else's job, out loud, for the first time.
lines.why: You stop the cash-in on herself and ask for the need. Once the need is said, Sam has something to answer, and the count loses its hold.

lines.text: “Fine. Cover it. You're good at that.”
lines.outcome: She says thanks, a bit flat, and goes to bed early.
lines.why: Warm words, but they hand her the chore again, so the coupon goes back in the bag.

lines.text: “Right, I'll do everything, as always. Don't mind me.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. She shuts her bedroom door, and the flat goes silent.
lines.why: This is the cash-in on herself. The coupon is spent on her own back, and the trap gets a fresh round tomorrow.

items.payoff: Friday, 6:40pm. Maya cashes the whole menu at once, on Sam and then on herself. The milk turns again in the fridge, and the rent arrives a day late.

fallout.them: Sam takes his keys and leaves the flat without speaking to her.

items.text: “Mum's notebook and Maya's menu are doing the same job. What are they, and what would a plain ask have looked like?”
items.cue: tapping the table once, twice, then leaving her hand flat on it
options: They are trading stamps: grudges kept back in a private book and waiting for a cash-in. A plain ask would have named the feeling and the want as they happened.
They are plain complaints about the day. The right reply would have answered each complaint and let it go.
They are honest feelings, so the right move was to agree with each one and move on.
items.why: Plain words first: these are grudge coupons. The books call them trading stamps, and a stamp is a feeling saved up instead of said, to be traded in later for a blow-up, on someone else or on yourself. A plain ask names the feeling and the want when they happen, so there is nothing left to keep.

traps.1: Answering each complaint sounds fair, but it treats every line as a single day. Mum and Maya would each hear that the day was dealt with. The book would stay open, and the cash-in would still arrive later in the week.
traps.2: Agreeing and moving on keeps the count hidden. The stamp stays in the book, and the feeling is agreed away instead of asked for.

items.example:
A cousins' group chat, Thursday.
Kate: “Fine. I'll sort the snacks, like always.”
Ruth: “Are you cross, or are you tired?”
Kate: “Tired. Ask me on Sunday.”

debrief.nadia: Almost nobody in those scenes raised their voice, and the book still filled up every day. Each line that was kept back waited for its day, and that day is when the payoff came. The way to stop the count is to ask for the want while it is still small.
debrief.bookNote: The books call these trading stamps: feelings saved up instead of said at the time, then traded in for a payoff on someone else, or on yourself.

reflection.prompt: Which grudge did you keep back this week, and who were you planning to cash it in on?
